questions.question: What does sync.WaitGroup do, and how do Go, Add, Done, and Wait work?
questions.title: How sync.WaitGroup tracks task completion
questions.direct_answer: A sync.WaitGroup tracks unfinished tasks and lets one goroutine wait until their count reaches zero. In current Go, WaitGroup.Go starts and tracks a function. Existing code often calls Add before launching a goroutine, defers Done inside it, and calls Wait after all tasks are registered. A WaitGroup coordinates completion; it does not protect shared data or carry results.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can explain the WaitGroup counter, current Go method, and its limited responsibility.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The zero value of sync.WaitGroup is ready to use.
WaitGroup.Go starts a task and removes it when the function returns.
The older pattern is Add before go, defer Done inside, then Wait.
Wait blocks until the task counter becomes zero.
A WaitGroup neither protects shared memory nor transports errors or values.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`sync.WaitGroup` is a task-completion primitive. Internally it behaves like a counter: starting tracked work increases the count, completing work decreases it, and `Wait` blocks until the count reaches zero. Its zero value is usable, so a normal declaration does not need a constructor.

In Go 1.25 and later, `wg.Go(f)` is the preferred way to start a goroutine that belongs to the group. It adds the task, starts `f` in a new goroutine, and removes the task when `f` returns. The documentation requires that `f` must not panic.

Older and still valid code uses `wg.Add(1)` before the `go` statement, followed by `defer wg.Done()` at the start of the goroutine. `Done` is equivalent to `Add(-1)`. Calling `Wait` after task registration holds the caller until every tracked task has finished.

For example, three goroutines can square three input values into separate slice positions. The main goroutine calls `Wait` before reading the complete result. Those separate element writes do not conflict, and completion of each task is ordered before the `Wait` that it releases.

A WaitGroup is not a lock, result collection, error group, or cancellation signal. If tasks mutate one shared map, that map still needs a mutex or single owner. If one task fails, the program needs an explicit error channel or a higher-level group. I use WaitGroup when the exact question is simply: have all these tasks finished?

sections.title: Think in unfinished tasks, not goroutines
sections.content: WaitGroup can track any finite set of tasks. A task is often a goroutine, but Add and Done can represent other completion events too. The important contract is that the group knows a task exists before a zero-count Wait is allowed to return.

sections.title: Build the counter and memory-ordering model
sections.content:
A newly declared WaitGroup has a counter of zero. `Wait` on that empty group returns immediately. Adding one task changes the count to one; completing it changes the count back to zero and releases waiters. If a negative Add makes the counter less than zero, the operation panics because the bookkeeping no longer represents a valid set of unfinished tasks.

Current Go offers two registration styles. `Go` covers the common case in which the group itself starts a new goroutine. Add and Done expose the counter directly and remain useful when adapting established code or tracking work started through another mechanism. Both styles require a clear boundary between registering a batch and waiting for it.

Completion also has a visibility guarantee. A `Done` call synchronizes before the return of a `Wait` that it unblocks; `WaitGroup.Go` gives the same guarantee for the return from its function. Therefore, after `Wait` returns, the waiting goroutine can observe results written by the completed tasks, provided the tasks did not race with one another while producing those results.

That last condition matters. WaitGroup orders task completion with the waiter, but it does not serialize two workers that both append to the same slice or write the same map. Safe designs give each worker a distinct output slot, protect shared state with a lock, or send results to one collector over a channel.

A WaitGroup should be shared by pointer and must not be copied after its first use. Copying duplicates the bookkeeping state rather than creating another view of the same group. Treat it as one lifecycle object: register work, wait for completion, and reuse it only after the previous Wait calls have returned.

sections.title: WaitGroup task lifecycle
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Z[Counter 0] -->|Go or Add 1| O[Counter 1+]
  O -->|Task starts| W[Work runs]
  W -->|Return or Done| D[Counter decreases]
  D -->|Still above 0| W
  D -->|Reaches 0| R[Wait returns]
```

questions.question: Why must WaitGroup tasks be registered before Wait, and how can a WaitGroup be reused safely?
questions.title: WaitGroup ordering and safe reuse
questions.direct_answer: When a WaitGroup counter is zero, a positive Add must happen before Wait; otherwise Wait may return before the new task is registered. In the manual pattern, call Add before the go statement, not inside the goroutine. A WaitGroup may serve another independent batch only after every Wait for the previous batch has returned, and it must not be copied after use.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands the zero-counter ordering rule, registration race, and batch reuse boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A positive Add on a zero counter must happen before Wait.
In manual code, call Add before launching the goroutine.
Done must run exactly once for each unit added.
Start a new reuse batch only after previous Wait calls return.
Never copy a WaitGroup after its first use.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The critical WaitGroup ordering rule applies when its counter is zero: registration of positive work must happen before a `Wait`. If the caller reaches `Wait` while the counter is still zero, it is allowed to return immediately because the group does not yet know about a future task.

That is why the manual idiom calls `wg.Add(1)` in the launching goroutine before `go func()`. Putting Add inside the new goroutine creates a scheduling window: the caller may execute `Wait`, observe zero, and continue before the worker has even registered itself.

The counter must also balance. Each unit added needs exactly one `Done`, commonly deferred at the beginning of the worker so every normal return path decrements it. Too few Done calls can block Wait forever; an extra Done makes the counter negative and panics.

For example, a batch processor can call `Add(len(jobs))`, launch one goroutine per index, and let every worker write to its own result slot. Once Wait returns, that batch is finished. Only then may the same group register a separate second batch and wait again.

Reuse is safe between completed batches, not while old Wait calls and a fresh zero-to-positive Add overlap. The group must also remain one shared value rather than being passed by value. For newly written goroutine code, `WaitGroup.Go` removes the separate Add/Done pairing, but its first call on an empty group still needs to precede Wait.

sections.title: The dangerous window exists at zero
sections.content: When the count is already positive, tracked work may create more tracked work. The fragile transition is zero to positive: a concurrent Wait cannot predict a task that has not been registered. Batch boundaries make that transition explicit.

sections.title: Concept guide · WaitGroup ordering and safe reuse
sections.content:
Imagine two goroutines: launcher and worker. In unsafe code, launcher executes a `go` statement and immediately calls Wait. The scheduler may keep running launcher, so Wait reads a zero counter and returns. Only afterward does worker run Add. No primitive connects the supposed completion point to the newly registered work.

Safe manual code reverses those first two events. Launcher performs Add while it still controls sequencing, then starts worker. Now any later Wait sees a positive count until worker calls Done. A defer placed immediately after the worker begins protects early returns, although code must still avoid calling Done along a second path.

The relationship is bookkeeping, not a promise about when workers begin. A worker may start before the loop launches the next worker, or all workers may start later. Correct code depends only on registration happening before Wait and every registered task eventually being completed.

Reuse creates another zero boundary. After batch one reaches zero and all its Wait calls return, the object can track batch two. Registering batch two while an earlier Wait is still active makes the lifecycle ambiguous and violates the documented reuse rule. Separate WaitGroups are often clearer when two batches overlap.

Copying is a different failure. Passing a WaitGroup by value after use copies counters and internal synchronization state; Done may update the copy while Wait observes the original. Use a pointer when passing it to a helper, and run `go vet`, whose copylocks analysis can identify many accidental copies of synchronization values.

sections.title: Registration must close the zero-count window
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Counter is 0] --> B{Register before Wait?}
  B -- Yes --> C[Add work]
  C --> D[Launch worker]
  D --> E[Wait observes positive count]
  E --> F[Done reaches 0]
  F --> G[Wait returns]
  B -- No --> H[Wait may return early]
  H --> I[Worker registers too late]
```

questions.question: What is WaitGroup.Go, and when would you still use Add and Done?
questions.title: WaitGroup.Go versus Add and Done
questions.direct_answer: WaitGroup.Go, added in Go 1.25, starts a function in a new goroutine and tracks it until the function returns, avoiding a separate Add/Done pair. Its function must not panic. Add and Done remain useful for established manual patterns or tasks whose lifecycle is registered separately from creating a goroutine. Both approaches share the same Wait and no-copy rules.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner knows the current WaitGroup API without erasing valid Add/Done use cases.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Go starts and tracks the function as one task.
The function passed to WaitGroup.Go must not panic.
Add and Done still support manually registered task lifecycles.
Nested Go calls are allowed while the group is non-empty.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`WaitGroup.Go` is the modern convenience method for the most common WaitGroup pattern. It records one task, starts the supplied function in a new goroutine, and marks the task complete when that function returns. It arrived in Go 1.25, so older codebases naturally contain Add, go, and Done instead.

The first `Go` call on an empty group must happen before `Wait`, just like a positive Add at zero. Once the group is non-empty, a task started through Go may itself call `wg.Go` to create more tracked work. `Wait` returns only after the resulting task tree has finished.

The API states that the function passed to Go must not panic. A task that can turn a failure into an ordinary error should report that error through another mechanism. WaitGroup itself still has no error aggregation, cancellation, or return-value channel.

Add and Done remain legitimate when adapting code that already launches goroutines, when an external callback marks completion, or when a task is registered separately from where it runs. The safe manual sequence is Add before the event, then one Done on every completion path.

For example, one Go task can discover two independent sub-tasks and register them through the same group. A mutex can protect their shared result slice, while Wait handles only lifecycle. I prefer Go for fresh goroutine code because it removes an easy bookkeeping mismatch, and I use Add/Done when the lifecycle genuinely requires explicit control.

sections.title: Go removes ceremony, not responsibility
sections.content: WaitGroup.Go prevents forgetting the matching Done in the standard goroutine case. The caller still owns task boundaries, shared-state safety, error handling, and cancellation. Add and Done expose lower-level registration when those boundaries do not match one new goroutine call.

sections.title: Concept guide · WaitGroup.Go versus Add and Done
sections.content:
Before Go 1.25, the conventional wrapper contained three separate operations: increment the group, launch a goroutine, and defer the decrement. This pattern remains correct, but moving or forgetting one line can produce early completion, a permanent wait, or a negative-counter panic. WaitGroup.Go packages that exact lifecycle behind one call.

The function contract is intentionally narrow. It has no parameters or return value in its type, so closures capture input and separate channels or synchronized structures carry output. It must not panic. If a task returns an error, a project may use an error channel or a purpose-built group with cancellation rather than expecting WaitGroup to interpret failure.

Nested work is supported. When the group already contains a running task, that task may call Go again before it returns. The counter remains positive throughout registration, so a concurrent Wait cannot mistake the group for an empty batch. This is useful for bounded recursive discovery, though unbounded task creation still needs limits.

Manual Add and Done provide a broader counter abstraction. A callback system can Add when it schedules an operation and Done when a completion event arrives, even if this code did not directly execute a go statement. That flexibility also makes correctness the programmer's responsibility: the delta and completion calls must balance.

Version support is a practical boundary. A module whose go directive or deployment toolchain predates Go 1.25 cannot call WaitGroup.Go, so the established pattern remains necessary there. For a current toolchain, use Go when it precisely represents 'start this tracked goroutine,' and keep Add/Done for the cases that actually need separate registration.

sections.title: Two ways to register completion
sections.content:
| Need | `WaitGroup.Go` | `Add` + `Done` |
|---|---|---|
| Start one new goroutine | Preferred | Valid but more bookkeeping |
| Track an externally started task | Not a direct fit | Suitable |
| Automatic completion on return | Yes | Only with a matching Done |
| Function may let panic escape | No | Program still must define panic handling |
| Toolchain requirement | Go 1.25+ | All supported older versions |
